newsitem.title: UK: European debt futures bounce on EMU deal. [CORRECTED 11:07 GMT 14/12]
newsitem.headline: European debt futures bounce on EMU deal. [CORRECTED 11:07 GMT 14/12]

text.p: European debt futures sprang into life late on Friday, relieved to see that European Union heads of government had hammered out a deal on stability pact for countries joining a planned single currency in 1999.
Diplomats at the EU summit meeting in Dublin said all 15 countries had agreed a deal, meant to ensure budgetary discipline after the start of economic and monetary union (EMU).
Traders said debt markets were staging a reaction rally, with investors covering protective short positions established earlier in the day.
"The markets have taken it as a very positive step," said a futures broker on London's LIFFE floor.
"But you must remember that the market has been short all day on fear, worry and concern about this meeting. The volume has been thin so we're seeing exaggerated moves in all products."
March Bund futures, which spent most of the session in negative territory, powered ahead after news of the deal and were trading 23 basis points higher at 100.10 by 1640 GMT.
Italian BTPs and French notionnel futures also leapt up, trading 122 and 28 (corrects from 78) basis points higher respectively at 128.32 and 128.28 respectively.
In Britain, which has an opt-out clause on EMU, March gilt futures were 14/32 higher on the day at 109-01 by 1640 GMT.
The stability pact agreement stated EMU members would be exempt from fines if their economies shrunk by more than two percent in any one year, a measure which analysts said was relatively strict.
Politicians would have to rule whether to impose penalties if shrinkage of between 0.75 and 2.0 percent occurred.
"There is this discretionary area which is between minus 0.75 and minus two percent which I regard as pretty tough," said Glenn Davies, chief UK economist at Credit Lyonnais in London.

Analysts said the deal should be encouraging for the Bund market with German Finance Minister Theo Waigel saying the pact would ensure that the euro will be a hard currency. "The fact that the two percent is in there will give a psychological advantage to the Germans," said Brian Venables senior bond strategist at ABN AMRO HOare Govett in Amsterdam.
